title: Foot-ring wax resist technique
subtitle: Using wax to protect the foot-ring and base from glaze before kiln loading
excerpt: Applying wax resist to a bisque-fired foot-ring prevents glaze from adhering to the areas that must remain bare for kiln loading. Wax resist is faster than wiping glaze by hand and produces a cleaner glaze line. It is used on every piece that has a foot-ring or requires a bare base.
sourceNotes: Foot-ring wax resist technique derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A water-based wax emulsion painted onto bisqueware to repel glaze; burns off cleanly during firing
First-fired porous clay; the stage at which wax resist is applied before glaze
The trimmed ridge the pot sits on; must be bare of glaze to prevent the pot from fusing to the kiln shelf
Pyrometric measure of heat-work. Cone 6 approx 1220 degrees C

content.text: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no dry sanding indoors. Adequate ventilation when firing. Do not open a hot kiln below 80 degrees C.
Every stoneware piece that goes into a kiln needs glaze kept clear of the
foot-ring
and base. Glaze that touches the kiln shelf fuses both together permanently.
Wax resist
is more reliable than wiping with a damp sponge because it creates a physical barrier that glaze cannot penetrate. The wax burns out during firing leaving no residue.
What you need
Water-based wax resist emulsion
A bisque-fired piece with a trimmed foot-ring
A liner brush dedicated to wax (wax will dry in the bristles and cannot be fully removed)
Banding wheel for rotating the piece while waxing
Step-by-step
Place the
bisque
-fired piece on the banding wheel.

Load the liner brush with wax resist and apply a band of wax around the foot-ring, covering the entire width of the ring and extending 3-5 mm up the side wall and across the base inside the ring. The wax should be visible as a white or milky coat.
Allow the wax to dry for 5-10 minutes. Test by touching lightly: dry wax has lost its milky appearance and feels slightly tacky but not wet.
Apply glaze to the piece as normal , by dipping, pouring, or brushing. The waxed areas will repel the glaze; glaze will bead and slide off them. Do not try to paint glaze over the waxed areas.
Check after glazing: wipe any glaze that has crept over the wax line with a clean damp sponge. The wax is resistant to one pass with a sponge but will come off if scrubbed repeatedly.
Load the piece on the kiln shelf. Fire to your target
cone
. The wax burns off between 200-500 degrees C during the firing ramp, long before the glaze melts.
What to check before kiln loading

Before loading, run a finger along the foot-ring. It should feel dry and smooth , no glaze residue. If you feel any grit or see any colour on your finger, the foot-ring has glaze on it. Wipe with a damp sponge before loading.

rows.problem: Glaze crept under the wax line and still on the foot-ring
rows.cause: Wax was applied too thinly, or glaze was dipped very forcefully and displaced the wax
rows.fix: Apply two coats of wax, allowing drying time between coats. For dip-glazing, lower into the glaze slowly.

rows.problem: Wax came off when wiping with a sponge post-glaze
rows.cause: Wax had not fully dried before glazing, or was scrubbed rather than wiped
rows.fix: Allow wax to dry fully before glazing , at least 15 minutes at room temperature. Use a single-pass wipe, not back-and-forth scrubbing.
